WHO interim guidance (version 1.2, 13 March 2020): Clinical management of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) when COVID-19 disease is suspected. Written for clinicians caring for adult, pregnant and paediatric patients with severe respiratory infection and critical illness. Although COVID-19-specific, its oxygen-therapy, ARDS, shock and complication-prevention sections are broadly applicable ICU supportive-care guidance.

OXYGEN THERAPY: Give supplemental oxygen immediately to patients with SARI and respiratory distress, hypoxaemia or shock. Initiate oxygen at 5 L/min and titrate to target SpO2 of 94% or higher during resuscitation; use a face mask with reservoir bag at 10 to 15 L/min for critically ill patients. Once stable, target SpO2 above 90% in non-pregnant adults and 92 to 95% in pregnant patients; in children with emergency signs target 94% or higher, otherwise 90% or higher. For acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure despite conventional oxygen, consider high-flow nasal cannula; if no improvement within 1 to 2 hours, proceed to timely intubation.

ARDS MANAGEMENT: Use lung-protective ventilation: tidal volumes 4 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight and plateau pressures below 30 cmH2O. In severe ARDS, prone positioning for more than 12 hours per day is recommended; consider ECMO where available if prone positioning fails. Use a conservative fluid strategy when there is no shock, since aggressive fluids worsen oxygenation.

SEPTIC SHOCK: Give empiric antimicrobials within 1 hour of identifying sepsis. Septic shock is defined as persisting hypotension despite volume resuscitation requiring vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) at 65 mmHg or higher, with serum lactate above 2 mmol/L. Use norepinephrine as the first vasopressor of choice in adults.

COMPLICATION PREVENTION: Apply daily awakening and spontaneous breathing trials, early mobilization, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, and glycaemic control. Corticosteroids were NOT routinely recommended for viral pneumonia outside trials in this edition. Care for pregnant patients should account for physiologic adaptations while applying the same supportive principles.
title: WHO — Clinical management of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI): interim guidance
